did.unittitle: Boris Schleifer Kingston Avenue Hospital album
did.abstract: Pages from an album of black and white photographs of Kingston Avenue Hospital taken by Boris Schleifer in 1925-1926 with handwritten captions.

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: Source and date of acquisition unknown. The collection was formally accessioned in 2020.

arrangement.p: The album pages are foldered in page number order.

bioghist.head: Historical note
bioghist.p: The Kingston Avenue Hospital was originally built as a so-called "pest house," or a place for isolating people suffering from contagious diseases such as smallpox and leprosy, in 1889 in the Flatbush area of what was then the city of Brooklyn. Following various complaints from patients, staff, and neighbors, the facility was improved in late 1895-early 1896 and renamed the Kingston Avenue Hospital. The hospital continued to treat Brooklynites with contagious diseases until 1955, when it was absorbed into the adjacent Kings County Hospital Center.

bioghist.head: Biographical note
bioghist.p: Boris Schleifer was born around 1886 to Isaac and Fannie Schleifer in Russia. He worked as an electrician before earning his medical degree from the Long Island College Hospital in 1924. He married Ray Feldman and they had a daughter, Evelyn. In 1932, he was fined for falsifying records of liquor prescriptions. In 1946, he was sentenced to two years in prison for illegally selling morphine sulphate tablets and consequently, lost his medical license in 1947.

processinfo.p: The collection was digitized and described on the item level at some point, likely in the early 2000s or 2010s. The collection was rehoused and this finding aid created by Dee Bowers in 2026.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Pages from an album of black and white photographs of Kingston Avenue Hospital taken by Boris Schleifer in 1925-1926 with handwritten captions. The photographs are mounted on black paper and the captions and page numbers are written in white ink. Some pages have captions but no image. The hospital buildings, facilities, ambulances, staff, and patients are depicted and labeled.
